pages.ja:
月の綺麗な夜だった。
自分は何をするでもなく、父である衛宮切嗣と月見をしている。
冬だというのに、気温はそう低くはなかった。
縁側はわずかに肌寒いだけで、月を肴にするにはいい夜だった。

pages.en:
The moon was beautiful that night.

I was doing nothing in particular, merely sitting with my father, Kiritsugu Emiya, and looking up at it.

Despite the season, the night was not terribly cold.

There was only a faint chill on the veranda. It was a good night to sit with the moon for company.

pages.ja:
この頃、切嗣は外出が少なくなっていた。
あまり外に出ず、家にこもってのんびりとしている事が多くなった。
……今でも、思い出せば後悔する。
それが死期を悟った動物に似ていたのだと、どうして気が付かなかったのか。

pages.en:
By then, Kiritsugu had stopped going out as often.

He rarely left the house. More and more, he remained at home and passed the days in peace.

…Even now, the memory fills me with regret.

Why did I never realize that he resembled an animal that knows its death is near?

pages.ja:
「子供の頃、僕は正義の味方に憧れてた」
ふと。
自分から見たら正義の味方そのものの父は、懐かしむように、そんな事を呟いた。

自分から見たら正義の味方そのものの父は、懐かしむように、そんな事を呟いた。
pages.en:
“When I was a child, I wanted to become a hero of justice.”

Without warning,

my father—who had always seemed the very image of a hero of justice to me—murmured those words with nostalgia.

pages.ja:
「なんだよそれ。憧れてたって、諦めたのかよ」
むっとして言い返す。
切嗣はすまなそうに笑って、遠い月を仰いだ。
pages.jaRuby:
「なんだよそれ。憧れてたって、諦めたのかよ」
むっとして言い返す。
切嗣はすまなそうに笑って、遠い月を仰いだ。
pages.en:
“What’s that supposed to mean? You *wanted* to? Did you give up?”

I bristled as I answered.

Kiritsugu smiled apologetically and raised his eyes toward the distant moon.

pages.ja:
「うん、残念ながらね。ヒーローは期間限定で、オトナになると名乗るのが難しくなるんだ。そんなコト、もっと早くに気が付けば良かった」
言われて納得した。
なんでそうなのかは分からなかったが、切嗣の言うことだから間違いないと思ったのだ。
pages.jaRuby:
「うん、残念ながらね。ヒーローは期間限定で、オトナになると名乗るのが難しくなるんだ。そんなコト、もっと早くに気が付けば良かった」
言われて納得した。
なんでそうなのかは分からなかったが、切嗣の言うことだから間違いないと思ったのだ。
pages.en:
“Yes, I’m afraid so. Being a hero is for a limited time. Once you grow up, it becomes difficult to call yourself one. I wish I had realized that sooner.”

His answer made sense to me.

I did not understand *why* it was true, but Kiritsugu had said it, and I believed he could not be wrong.

pages.ja:
「そっか。それじゃしょうがないな」
「そうだね。本当に、しょうがない」
相づちをうつ切嗣。
だから当然、俺の台詞なんて決まっていた。
pages.jaRuby:

pages.en:
“I see. Then I suppose there’s nothing you can do.”

“No. There really isn’t.”

Kiritsugu agrees.

And so, naturally, there is only one thing I can say.

pages.ja:
「うん、しょうがないから俺が代わりになってやるよ。
爺さんはオトナだからもう無理だけど、俺なら大丈夫だろ。まかせろって、爺さんの夢は」

pages.en:
“Then I’ll take your place. You’re a grown-up now, old man, so it’s too late for you. But I can still do it.

“Leave your dream to me—”

pages.ja:
“
俺が、ちゃんと形にしてやるから”
pages.jaRuby:
“
俺が、ちゃんと形にしてやるから”
pages.en: *I’ll make it real for you.*

続きなんて聞くまでもないっていう顔だった。
衛宮切嗣はそうか、と長く息を吸って、
「ああ
安心した」
静かに目蓋を閉じて、その人生を終えていた。

Before I can finish saying it, my father smiles.

His expression tells me there is no need to hear the rest.

Kiritsugu Emiya draws one long breath and says,

“Ah—what a relief.”

Then he quietly closes his eyes and brings his life to an end.

それが、朝になれば目覚めるような穏やかさだったから、幼い自分は騒ぎ立てなかった。
死というものを見慣れていた事もあったのだろう。
何をするでもなく、冬の月と、長い眠りに入った、父親だった人を見上げていた。

He died with the same peace as someone falling asleep, certain they would wake in the morning. The child I was did not raise an alarm.

Perhaps I had simply seen death too many times.

I did nothing. I looked up at the winter moon and at the man who had been my father, now entered into a long sleep.

pages.ja:
庭には虫の声もなく、あたりは静かだった。
明るい夜の中、両目だけが熱かったのを覚えている。
泣き声もあげず、悲しいと思う事もない。
月が落ちるまで、ただ、涙だけが止まらなかった。

No insects called in the garden. Everything around us was silent.

In that brilliant darkness, I remember that only my eyes felt hot.

I did not sob. I did not even feel sad.

Until the moon sank, only the tears refused to stop.

それが五年前の冬の話。
むこう十年分ぐらい泣いたおかげか、その後はサッパリしたものだった。

pages.en:
That happened one winter, five years ago.

Perhaps I cried enough that night to last the next ten years. Afterward, I felt remarkably clear.

切嗣がいなくなっても変わらない。

Fuji’s father arranged the funeral, and I began living alone in the Emiya house.

Nothing changed when Kiritsugu disappeared.

Shirou Emiya intended to become a hero of justice like him. There was no time to idle.

pages.ja:
そう。
口にはしなかったけど、ちゃんと覚えていたんだ。
十年前、火事場に残されていた自分を救い出してくれた男の姿を。
意識もなく、全身に火傷を負って死にかけていた子供を抱き上げて、目に涙をためるぐらい喜んで、外に連れ出してくれた。

—Yes.

I never spoke of it, but I remembered perfectly.

I remembered the man who rescued me when I was left behind in the fire ten years ago.

He lifted a dying child from the flames—unconscious, burned over his whole body—and carried him outside with tears of joy in his eyes.

pages.ja:
その時から、彼は俺の憧れになった。
誰も助けてくれなかった。
誰も助けてやれなかった。
その中でただ一人助けられた自分と、ただ一人助けてくれた人がいた。
だから、そういう人間になろうと思ったのだ。

From that moment, he became the person I admired.

No one else saved us.

No one else could save anyone.

Amid all of that, there was one person who was saved, and one person alone who saved him.

—That was why I decided to become someone like him.

pages.ja:
彼のように誰かを助けて、誰も死なせないようにする正義の味方に。
その彼こそが“そういうモノ”に成りたかったと遺して、自分の前で穏やかに幕を閉じた。

A hero of justice who would save people as he had, who would allow no one to die.

Then that man left behind the confession that he, too, had wanted to become *such a thing*, and quietly lowered the curtain before my eyes.

pages.ja:
子が父の跡を継ぐのは当然のこと。
衛宮士郎は正義の味方になって、かつての自分のような誰かを助けなくてはいけない。
幼い頃にそう誓った。
誰よりも憧れたあの男の代わりに、彼の夢を果たすのだと。

pages.en:
It is only natural for a child to carry on his father’s work.

Shirou Emiya has to become a hero of justice and save someone like the boy he once was.

I swore it as a child.

In place of the man I admired above all others, I would fulfill his dream.

切嗣の言っていた正義の味方ってどんなモノなのかとか、早く一人前になる方法とか、切嗣の口癖だったみんなが幸せでいられればいい、なんて魔法みたいな夢の実現方法とか、それと、マスターなんてモノになっちまって、一緒に付いてきた金髪の女の子とか頭んなかがゴチャゴチャだ、ホント

…Though honestly, I understand very little.

What sort of thing Kiritsugu meant by a hero of justice, how I am supposed to become a real mage quickly, how anyone could realize that impossible dream he always spoke of where everybody gets to be happy, and now I have somehow become something called a Master and there is a blond girl following me around and my head is a complete mess, honestly—

「……う……口ん中、まずい……」

“………”

I open my eyes in my familiar room.

“…Ugh… My mouth tastes awful…”

The taste is of old, stagnant blood.

Perhaps blood pooled inside my mouth as I slept. Every breath draws in thick, clotted air.

“—Hup.”

I sit up.

The room spins.

I nearly collapse and catch myself against the wall.

“…Ugh.”

Movement worsens the nausea.

…No. This is closer to agony than nausea.

My body feels leaden, and every movement sends my insides churning. If someone poured molten lead into my stomach, I imagine it would feel much like this.

“…Hot… I imagined it too vividly, and now I’m running a fever.”

I wipe the sweat from my forehead and stagger out of the room with one hand against the wall.

“…All right. That’s a little better.”

I wash my face, then wipe the sweat from my body while I am here.

“…?”

For some reason, bandages are wrapped around my abdomen.

I cannot imagine why, so I set the question aside for now.

“Ngh…”

I steel myself and begin edging along the wall.

The dizziness has not improved, and more than anything, my body feels slow.

“Ow—ow, ow…”

I advance with a pathetic whimper.

…What on earth did I do before going to sleep?

I certainly do not remember training hard enough to leave every muscle in my body aching.

I reach the living room.

Sakura and Fuji must both be at school today.

There is no breakfast waiting and no Fuji making her usual commotion.

The silent room looks like any other Sunday morning—

“Good morning. I let myself in, Emiya.”

—No. It does not.

With no idea how to respond, I settle onto a floor cushion.

Then I take a deep breath and say—

“—You’re definitely consuming *something*.

“Your lifespan, your luck, your bank balance—whatever it is, something must be draining away at a terrifying rate.”

Tohsaka gives another indignant snort.

I cannot entirely disagree.

“I refuse to accept a world where it works any other way—especially for me!”

Rin Tohsaka erupts in a pillar of purely personal resentment.

What am I going to do now? I am the one who wants an answer to that.

That means forcing Servants to kill one another.

I thought the matter could end if the Masters reached an understanding and renounced the Holy Grail together. But if Servants answered their summons because they desire the Grail and will never relinquish it, then conflict between them cannot be avoided after all.

…Then—

the girl who fought to protect me must also struggle over the Holy Grail, killing and being killed.

I came to terms with that long ago. I understand it.

Even so, I am not strong enough to weigh the life and death of another human being on a scale of good and evil.

More troublesome still, Servants ordinarily exist in spiritual form.

Anyone without spiritual sensitivity cannot even perceive them.

Yet they can interfere with the physical world as though they possess bodies. By that fact alone, a Servant could be called the ultimate weapon.

Modern science has no weapon capable of harming a spiritual entity.

To an ordinary person, death at a Servant’s hands would resemble a natural disaster.

When an invisible killer attacks, its victim’s death can only be recorded as an accident or suicide.

“There is one detail I neglected to mention. Servants are spirits. Their existence is already complete, so they cannot grow beyond their present limits.

“But magical energy, the fuel they consume, is another matter.

“The more magical energy a Servant accumulates, the more freely they can employ the extraordinary abilities they possessed in life.

“In that respect they resemble us mages… Do you understand what that implies?”

pages.jaRuby: 「解る。魔術を連発できるって事だろ」
pages.en: “Yes. They can use magecraft repeatedly.”

銃の種類は短銃、ライフル銃、マシンガン、ショットガンと、魔術師ごとに性能が異なる。

Magical energy is the gunpowder packed into a cartridge. A mage is the gun.

The type of weapon varies according to the mage’s capabilities: handgun, rifle, machine gun, shotgun.

In that analogy, Servants are not guns at all. They are cannons.

By consuming an enormous quantity of powder, they fire an enormous shell.

“Precisely. But Servants do not receive magical energy—Mana—from nature as we do. As a rule, they operate only on the energy contained within themselves.

“We Masters replenish that supply. A Servant can exercise no more of their former power than their own magical energy plus whatever is furnished by the Master who commands them.”

“Servants are spiritual entities. If they consume something of the same nature, it provides nourishment.”

As we eat flesh, they, as human spirits—

“And if a Master commits murder openly, the Association will intervene. Worse, the manner of death may expose the Servant’s powers and identity to the other Masters—and, naturally, the Master’s identity as well.

“Concealing who you are provides an overwhelming advantage in the Holy Grail War. Any ordinary Master should avoid revealing their Servant unless absolutely necessary.”

At the very least, I have no way to stop a monster like that.
